terms.name: LoCo
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report math and code experiments. These results have not been independently reproduced by this app.
terms.meaning: LoCo trains a reasoning model to decide whether to continue reasoning or conclude from its current state.

how.title: Find likely overthinking
how.detail: Locate reasoning states where a shorter continuation might already reach a correct answer.

how.title: Create a local comparison
how.detail: Freeze each prefix and generate shorter, verified continuations from that same state.

how.title: Train the stopping decision
how.detail: Use DPO on state-conditioned preference pairs, teaching when to stop rather than imposing one length target on every problem.

terms.why: Reasoning length affects response time and serving cost. Efficiency matters only if the model preserves correctness on your actual tasks.
terms.example: A math assistant could learn to stop after a sufficient derivation instead of adding redundant checks. The method requires training access and verified examples.
terms.experiment: Inspect the accuracy–length tradeoff on ten verifiable problems before attempting to train a stopping policy.
terms.caution: The paper studies particular math and code benchmarks. The POC explores stopping decisions and does not reproduce LoCo’s DPO training.

source.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

poc.goal: Find where shorter reasoning stops being sufficient on ten problems.
requirements: Ten math or code problems with independently checked answers
An open reasoning model exposing generated traces, or public examples from the paper
A spreadsheet for correctness, output length and elapsed time
steps: Collect a complete trace and answer for each problem, using fixed prompts and sampling settings.
Choose two plausible stopping points in each trace. Ask the same model to finish from each prefix.
Check every answer against the independent answer or executable tests. Record length and time.
Compare shorter correct continuations with the baseline and inspect every failure.
successCriteria: Every claimed improvement retains a verified correct final answer.
Report length and correctness together for all ten problems, including failures.
poc.limitations: This is a diagnostic exercise, without preference-pair training. It cannot establish the paper’s reported model improvements.

terms.name: ToolSpace
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report replay-verified environments and benchmark experiments. Transfer beyond those environments remains to be established.
terms.meaning: ToolSpace builds agent training and evaluation environments from dependencies observed between real tool calls, then turns replayable sequences into tasks.

how.title: Build a tool graph
how.detail: Extract data, state and retry dependencies from adjacent tool calls in execution traces.

how.title: Construct environments
how.detail: Cluster connected tools. Synthesize databases for state-mutating tools and replay recorded returns for query or stateless tools.

how.title: Verify generated tasks
how.detail: Use state-aware walks and rollback, translate successful chains into tasks, and keep those whose outcome assertions replay from the starting state.

terms.why: Your tool traces can help reveal workflow failures that isolated tool-call tests miss. Repeatable state and executable checks are central to a useful evaluation.
terms.example: A mock support task could retrieve a customer, update a ticket and verify the final ticket state. Every replay starts from a clean snapshot.
terms.experiment: Build five replayable evaluation tasks from tool traces in a mock support workspace.
terms.caution: Trace-derived environments inherit the coverage and biases of the traces. This small POC illustrates the idea and does not reproduce the full synthesis or training pipeline.

source.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents

poc.goal: Create five tasks with clean starting states and repeatable outcome checks.
requirements: A mock ticket database or JSON file with no production data
Five successful traces with tool names, arguments and returns
A script to reset state and replay calls
steps: Record five workflows against the mock workspace, including reads and state changes.
Connect calls where a returned value becomes a later argument, and record separate state dependencies.
Write initial snapshots and final assertions, then describe each task without revealing the tool sequence.
Replay every task twice from clean state, then compare an agent’s final assertions with the baseline.
successCriteria: Every retained task produces identical outcome assertions on two clean replays.
Report agent task success separately from environment replay reliability.
poc.limitations: Five inspected traces cannot establish the full method’s environment coverage, benchmark difficulty, or training benefits.

terms.name: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning
terms.meaning: A research approach that trains a speculative draft model to disagree at important reasoning points, causing target verification to restart there. It uses rejection timing to manage numerical precision during long agent tasks.

how.title: Find sensitive decision points
how.detail: The authors examine where numerical differences within speculative verification windows can affect later agent decisions.

how.title: Train for selective disagreement
how.detail: Their draft model learns adversarial preferences around these points, seeking useful rejections rather than maximizing acceptance everywhere.

how.title: Restart target verification
how.detail: Draft disagreement restarts verification at selected points. The authors report coding benchmark gains under their evaluated settings.

terms.why: For a PM, decoding speed and task success can interact. Evaluate an acceleration method on completed tasks as well as tokens per second.
terms.example: A coding-agent evaluation could compare task pass rates and runtime across speculative-decoding configurations, rather than choosing the highest draft acceptance rate alone.
terms.experiment: Use a small rounding simulation to explore why numerical settings can affect repeated decisions. This is a diagnostic exercise, not an ASR reproduction.
terms.caution: The evidence comes from the authors’ long-horizon coding experiments. Results on other tasks and runtimes remain uncertain. Reproducing ASR requires model and inference-engine work beyond this exercise.

source.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents

terms.evidenceNote: The authors report coding experiments with trained draft models. This app has not reproduced those results.

poc.goal: See how rounding and restart intervals can change a chain of toy decisions.
requirements: A spreadsheet or Python with its standard library
A table with columns for step, reference value, rounded value, decision and mismatch
steps: Create 40 rows. Start two values at 0.4. At each row compute next = 3.9 × value × (1 − value). Keep one column at full precision; round the other to three decimal places after each update.
Record a toy decision at every row: A if the value is at least 0.5, B otherwise. Count disagreements between the two columns.
Repeat with restart windows of 4, 8 and 16 rows. At each boundary copy the current reference value into the rounded column, then continue updating.
Repeat all settings from starting values 0.2 and 0.7. Keep every result, including settings where restarting does not reduce disagreement.
successCriteria: Record the first disagreement and total mismatched decisions across all 40 rows for each of the three starting values.
Produce a comparison table for the three restart windows and the no-restart baseline; account for every trial without claiming an agent accuracy gain.
poc.limitations: This toy recurrence illustrates numerical sensitivity and resets. It contains no draft model, target model, learned rejection policy or real agent task, so it cannot test ASR performance.

terms.generatedBy: AI-written · source and POC checked · suggested exercise

terms.name: In-context learning
terms.meaning: In-context learning lets a pretrained model infer a task from demonstrations in its prompt, without changing its weights. A recent circuit study examines how a label memory, class-matching attention and a repetition signal support this behavior in a controlled sentence-classification setting.

how.title: Store the demonstrated labels
how.detail: In the studied models, each label position carries the label identity in its residual stream. Middle-layer heads write the preceding demonstration’s class as a key at that position.

how.title: Match the query class
how.detail: Upper-layer heads match the query’s class against those stored keys and copy the corresponding label values.

how.title: Enable the readout
how.detail: An early signal indicates that a label has repeated. Without that signal, readers attend to the prompt’s start and no label is favored.

how.title: Keep a separate recency effect
how.detail: Other heads suppress the most recently seen label. The paper treats this as a separate component, rather than the repetition gate.

terms.why: This gives builders a specific hypothesis for prompt experiments: demonstrations can supply a temporary label mapping. Test example choice and label assignments on your own tasks before assuming that more context will help.
terms.example: Demonstrations can map the classes cat and dog to arbitrary labels such as dax and wug. A new query’s class can then retrieve the demonstrated label mapping during the forward pass.
terms.experiment: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
terms.caution: The circuit evidence comes from controlled classification experiments in three small transformers, with additional tests within one model family. The toy below does not establish how other models or production tasks behave.
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report activation patching, head ablations and steering experiments. This app has not reproduced their neural-circuit results.

poc.goal: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
requirements: Python 3 with its standard library, or a spreadsheet
Three label sets: A = dax,wug,dax; B = dax,wug,zop; C = wug,dax,wug
steps: For each label set, run two queries: (1,0) and (0,1). Calculate the dot product of the query and each of the three class-key vectors. These are hand-chosen class features, not model activations.

Build an ungated baseline: sum the matching scores for each label, then divide by the total score to make a label distribution. For A, the first query gives dax a total score of 2 and wug a score of 0.

Add the repetition gate: if any label repeats in the demonstration set, retain the baseline distribution. If every label is unique, return an equal distribution over the unique labels instead. This models the source’s presence-versus-absence condition in a simplified way.
Compare A with B to inspect the gate, then A with C to inspect relabeling. Keep the class keys and queries fixed. Record all six outputs and their ungated baselines.
successCriteria: Across the four repeated-label query cases in A and C, the highest-scoring labels follow each set’s demonstrated mapping. Relabeling A to C changes both query predictions without changing the class keys.
For both all-unique cases in B, the gated version returns 1/3 for each of its three labels, while the ungated baseline is nonuniform. Omitting the gate must therefore fail this check.
poc.limitations: This hand-written lookup illustrates selected components. It uses no neural weights or attention heads, omits the separate recency-suppression effect, and cannot reproduce the paper’s causal interventions or measure a real model’s ICL performance.

items.title: claude-code · v2.1.319
items.summary: ## What's changed - Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about…
items.releaseNotes:
## What's changed

- Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0` to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
- Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1` turns on the server-side check even with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS` set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the `1` too
- Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
- Added the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND` environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
- Added `permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting` setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
- Added `/claude-api latency-optimize` to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
- Added the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS` environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
- Added spend for today, this week and this month to `/usage` for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
- Added `admin.pooled_conflict_rule` and `admin.pooled_priority_order` to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
- Added an optional `login_notice` setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
- Added `CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json` to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with `severity`, `time` and `message`, for log collectors that read the level from a field
- Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's `availableModels` also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
- Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no `desktopHome` that rely on `coworkTabEnabled: false` or `chatSessionRetentionDays`, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
- Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from `ant auth login`, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
- Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from `ant auth login`
- Added an "Earlier in this session" row to `/tasks` that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
- Added a note to `/loop` confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
- Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
- Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after `--resume`
- Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named `HEAD`
- Fixed `/diff` showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named `HEAD` at its top level
- Fixed the `/diff` pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
- Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running
- Fixed a request that kept failing with a 401 refreshing your login on every retry and causing 401s in your other sessions
- Fixed `/context` sending its full visual grid to Claude on every later turn; Claude now reads only the table
- Fixed `claude -p` exiting 0 in auto mode when its actions were refused because no safety check was available: text and JSON output now exit 1
- Fixed a case where Claude Code listed every project file at start on Linux for projects on a network file system (NFS, SMB, Lustre and similar)
- Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
- Fixed `/status` showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it
- Fixed Claude-drafted feedback, surveys and `/feedback` continuing to appear after the server refused feedback for your organization
- Fixed Claude drafting feedback on third-party gateways, where it can't be sent
- Fixed auto mode refusing actions without saying why when permission rules or `autoMode` settings are very large: it now explains and, unless `autoMode` deny rules are set, asks you in the terminal
- Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words
- Fixed subagent hand-back reports showing an internal marker and provenance note when expanded outside verbose mode
- Fixed `claude -p --resume` with a prompt losing a deferred tool call when its MCP server is missing: the run now exits 1, keeps the call and refuses later input
- Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients
- Fixed a case where Agent SDK hosts got a generic exit-code error instead of a failed run's own error message when the disk was full
- Fixed `CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN` re-running a turn that was interrupted in plan mode when the session resumes in another permission mode
- Fixed edits to a settings file being ignored when made within a few seconds of Claude Code writing that file
- Fixed a config file left at the legacy name hiding your setup with no warning: Claude Code now says on stderr when a home holds two config files, and which is in use
- Fixed `~/.claude.json`, settings and edited files ending up empty or cut off when the disk fills during a save in a read-only folder or to a bind-mounted file (one session saving at a time)
- Fixed Write ending the turn as a refusal when it couldn't read the file to overwrite
- Fixed background Bash commands that finish almost instantly losing their output while being reported as completed
- Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files missing a file that the command wrote just before it ended
- Fixed a mistyped model name, such as `opus-5-5`, telling you to update Claude Code instead of suggesting the model you meant
- Fixed a case where `NotebookEdit` changed the wrong cell when the notebook changed while a permission prompt was open
- Fixed a ~0.5s hang after pressing Enter on the `/login` success screen: the dialog now dismisses immediately and the post-login refresh runs in the background
- Fixed Ctrl+G not opening the external editor while typing an "Other" answer to a question in screen reader mode
- Fixed Monitor's WebSocket watch failing with "could not resolve" behind a proxy when `CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS` is set and the machine has no DNS of its own
- Fixed `claude plugin eval` warnings suggesting `max: 0` for a tool that must not be called, which could never pass
- Fixed background plugin auto-update not installing a dependency added by the updated plugin version
- Fixed Cmd+click not opening links in Ghostty over tmux in sessions opened from the agents view
- Fixed a mod's hot reload in `.claude/skills` missing a file that was deleted just after it appeared, and missing its return
- Fixed `/rewind` failing with "No files were restored" when restoring code to a checkpoint from before `/branch`
- Fixed the `/claude-api` skill saying Console web settings don't apply to Managed Agents sessions, and tightened its credential and permission examples
- Fixed needless permission prompts for read-only commands wrapped in a plain `timeout DURATION`, such as `timeout 30 rg foo`
- Fixed WebFetch describing claude.ai shared-chat links as empty pages; it now says shared chats can't be read and to paste the conversation instead
- Fixed Artifact database calls being re-sent to artifacts without a database; errors now say whether republishing helps
- Fixed a case where artifact database reads that save to a folder (`out_dir`) were refused
- Fixed detailed beta tracing not presenting `CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT` to collectors that require a client certificate
- Fixed the OpenTelemetry `claude_code.session.count` metric counting Agent SDK `prewarm()` processes that were never claimed; a pre-started process now counts once, when it is claimed
- Fixed `/clear` killing running commands of background agents, teammates and workflows that keep running, and foreground subagents of background agents and teammates
- Fixed a terminal whose Claude apps gateway sign-in had expired sending telemetry and managed-settings requests that the gateway refused and logged as `invalid_token`
- Fixed the agents view appearing to send a reply to a background session waiting on a permission prompt; the reply now stays in the box with a hint to open the session and answer
- Fixed agent view removing a draft saved by another agent view in the same directory when exiting
- Fixed a case where agent view came back with another agent view's input text after restarting itself for an update
- Fixed the agents view preview cutting off long commands, results and status lines without an ellipsis, and dropping `**`, backticks and tags from commands waiting for approval
- Fixed Claude in Chrome reporting the extension as not connected when the connection dropped mid-action; Claude now checks the page before repeating an action that may have run
- Fixed Remote Control sessions still showing "Limit reached" on other devices after a usage limit was lifted outside the session
- Fixed the file card sometimes missing in the Claude iOS app when Claude sent a single file
- Fixed self-hosted runner sessions failing with no explanation when the server keeps refusing to renew model access: the runner now retries sooner and posts a warning in the session
- Fixed `/permissions` in cloud sessions replying only that it isn't available; it now says where the session's rules live and how to change them
- Fixed cloud sessions losing session-scoped deny and ask permission rules, such as those a PermissionRequest hook adds, when the session moves to a new worker
- Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the session when you typed three messages instead of answering its question in a cloud session
- Fixed background tasks that keep running after `/clear` disappearing from the task list in Claude Code on the web until another task started or ended
- Fixed hidden commands appearing in the slash command menu of cloud sessions on mobile and web
- Fixed a case where `/rewind` could restore or delete a file through a directory symlink
- Fixed a case where a `sed` command could skip the permission check in accept-edits and auto mode
- Fixed a case where `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1` in managed settings was ignored behind an LLM gateway when the gateway's URL is set only there and server-managed settings can't be fetched
- Fixed a Bash permission bypass where a crafted environment prefix could hide part of a command from permission checks
- Fixed a case where deny and ask rules, hook matchers and `disallowedTools` entries written with a claude.ai connector's terminal name (`mcp__claude_ai_Slack`) were ignored in Claude Desktop (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
- Fixed a sandbox escape when creating a worktree
- Fixed self-hosted runners: `--trust-workspace false` now also stops hooks in the repository's settings files and skills from running
- Fixed a case where idle background sessions started through a shell-exported LLM gateway left the gateway after an update
- Fixed help links in `/status` and the auto mode billing notice opening only part of the address when they wrap
- Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
- Fixed `claude remote-control` exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
- Fixed `claude remote-control` ignoring a piped `y` that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
- Fixed `/rename` reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
- Fixed `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` not being substituted in a plugin-provided `subagentStatusLine` command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
- Fixed `claude plugin update` and `/plugin` "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
- Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
- Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
- Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave `~/.claude.json` empty
- Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
- Improved Claude in Chrome: `javascript_tool` results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
- Improved `claude purge` and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
- Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
- Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in `/stats`, `/model` and `/sandbox`, and rejected-action messages
- Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
- Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
- Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then `admin.blocked_message` if one is set
- Improved the `/model` picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
- Improved `/context` at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called
- Improved `/usage` in cloud sessions: it now links to Settings → Usage on claude.ai in a case where plan limits can't be shown
- [VSCode] Improved the confirmation for removing a plugin marketplace: it now checks which of its plugins are installed at that moment
- Changed MCP tasks to work in the terminal without feature-flag fetching (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, LLM gateways, `DISABLE_TELEMETRY`); set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASKS=1` to turn them off

- Changed `CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS` so

items.releaseNotes:
## New Features

- Open the agent command center with `codex agents --no-daemon`. The command center and session picker now mark unread results (#58238, #58239, #58263, #58264).
- Switch between connected backends from the terminal session picker and keep your drafts when switching (#58280, #58457).
- Preview local image attachments while composing on supported terminals, and open viewed local images from clickable transcript paths (#58261, #58446).
- Find API key and cloud provider options under “Sign in another way.” Enable `gcp_setup_wizard` to set up Google Cloud Vertex AI with Application Default Credentials or a credential file (#57857, #58427).
- Opt into macOS or Windows system proxy settings from `/experimental` (#58157).
- Expand patch details directly in the transcript while an approval prompt is open (#58281).

## Bug Fixes

- Saved chats stay visible after you switch model providers. If a chat can’t resume, you can read its transcript and prepare an editable prompt to continue in a new chat (#58202).
- `Ctrl+L` clears the terminal display while keeping earlier messages available through `Ctrl+T` (#58266).
- Deleting text that exposes a leading `!` keeps an ordinary draft in chat mode (#58412).
- Network approval prompts close when their requests end. Concurrent requests to the same endpoint prompt one at a time (#58350, #58351).
- Long realtime V3 conversations save completed speech to chat history as the transcript grows (#58221).
- Automatic context compaction now accounts for retained output from failed responses and responses with missing token usage data (#58404).

## Documentation

- The app-server README covers managed network constraints under `[permissions.network]` and `prompt-user` command rules that require fresh human approval (#58045, #58182).
- The `openai-docs` skill recommends the documented replacement when migrating away from a deprecated model (#58134).

## Chores

- DotSlash manifests now reference the Cargo packages shipped with the release (#58717, #58757).
- Linux musl builds use fewer allocator arenas to reduce idle memory after conversations unload (#58399).

items.title: Agents Are Going Async
items.summary: Agent Architecture Open Source Agents Are Going Async Sydney Runkle Thushanth Bengre November 5, 2026 5 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents…
items.briefingSourceText: Agent Architecture Open Source Agents Are Going Async Sydney Runkle Thushanth Bengre November 5, 2026 5 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways As agents take on bigger goals, they need to stay responsive to the user while making progress on many long tasks at once. Async subagents split an agent into an orchestrator that stays available to the user and subagents that run tasks in the background and report back to the orchestrator upon completion. Background work is becoming the norm for agent infrastructure, from coding agents like Claude Code to personal agents like OpenAI's dots. Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. How async subagents work An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. The orchestrator hands work to async subagents and stays free to talk to the user. Async work depends on two properties of the system: The user can reach the orchestrator. The orchestrator is the agent the user interacts directly with. Subagents no longer hold its loop, so the user can reach it whenever its own loop isn't busy, instead of waiting for every subagent to finish. Tasks run in parallel without blocking. The orchestrator starts subagents as work comes in, instead of waiting for a whole batch to return. The orchestrator manages async subagents with five tools: start_async_task starts a subagent on its own thread and returns right away. check_async_task gets a task's status and, once it finishes, its result. update_async_task sends a running task new instructions. cancel_async_task stops a running task. list_async_tasks lists every task and its status. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: "interrupt" (the default) stops the current run and restarts the subagent with the new instruction. Use it for a correction like "use Postgres instead." "enqueue" holds the follow-up until the current run finishes. Use it for an addition like "run the tests when you're done." How notifications work Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : If the orchestrator is busy , it checks its unfinished tasks before each model call and picks up the result mid-run. If it's idle , the subagent wakes it with a new run. If it's paused on an approval, the approval is left alone, and the result arrives once the user answers. An async subagent reports back whether the orchestrator is busy, idle, or paused on an approval. A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. In Managed Deep Agents on Slack, the request posts back to the original thread . We expect this pattern to generalize beyond subagents to tools across the board. OpenAI recently added support for async tool calling , where the model keeps working after it calls a tool and your application sends the result back in a later request. Use async subagents Async subagents are available in Deep Agents for Python and JavaScript , and in Managed Deep Agents , where making a subagent async takes one field: from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent agent = define_deep_agent( name="research-assistant", model="openai:gpt-5.5", subagents=[ { "name": "researcher", "description": "Researches a topic in the background.", "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.", "async": True, }, ], ) In Managed Deep Agents, every served agent also gets an async copy of the general-purpose subagent, so it can decide at runtime whether to run delegated work in the foreground or the background. Task notifications are in beta, so the API may still change. The async-deep-agents repo has a working supervisor with researcher and coder subagents in Python and TypeScript. Give async subagents a try, and let us know what you think in GitHub issues or on the forum . Related content Deep Agents Agent Architecture How We Optimized

items.title: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation
SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
items.summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process…
items.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

items.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
items.summary: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared…
items.abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

items.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
items.summary: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA…
items.abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

items.title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
items.summary: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes,…
items.abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.

items.title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
items.summary: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found…
items.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

items.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed…
items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

items.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
items.summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend…
items.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

items.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.summary: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control.…
items.abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

items.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
items.summary: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to…
items.abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

items.title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
items.summary: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the…
items.abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

items.title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
items.summary: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet…
items.briefingSourceText: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.

items.title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying…
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.

items.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
items.summary: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated…
items.briefingSourceText: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958). We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves. More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

items.title: The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?
items.summary: The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv…
items.abstract: The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv papers, recent papers disclosing substantive AI use, and manuscripts released by OpenAI provide a rich empirical basis for studying this question. However, several challenges remain: lack of matched case-control pairs; potential incompleteness of disclosure; and lack of ready-to-use features designed to capture signals of AI involvement in proofs. To address these challenges, we construct five cohorts comprising 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with those we produced using generative AI. These cohorts span different levels of AI involvement and include matched pairs of papers addressing the same research problems. We then introduce ProofTrace, a framework that represents each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extracts interpretable features of mathematical organization. Our study yields three discoveries. First, principal-component projections of our features reveal a qualitative gradient of AI involvement, where AI-reworded papers remain close to human papers, the two AI-generated cohorts depart in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use occupy intermediate positions which shifts toward AI-generated cohorts over time. Second, we identify recurring signatures of AI-generated proofs, such as fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered graph connectivity; many of these signatures persist under controls for research field, manuscript length, or graph size. Finally, in a separate detection experiment, ProofTrace distinguishes human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use. Its performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas the performance of state-of-the-art text-based detectors declines sharply.

items.title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
items.summary: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its…
items.abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.

items.title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
items.summary: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates…
items.abstract: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

items.title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
items.summary: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across…
items.abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

items.title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
items.summary: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We…
items.abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

items.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
items.summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction…
items.aiSummary: A linear attention architecture called Muir allocates gate capacity by sensitivity, uses matched-filter readout and a stable parallel update, improving language modeling, long-context recall, and training speed over Gated DeltaNet-2 and Transformer baselines.
items.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

items.title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
items.summary: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely…
items.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.

items.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
items.summary: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal…
items.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

items.title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
items.summary: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding…
items.abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.

items.title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
items.summary: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling…
items.abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
